title: Psychotropic-induced weight gain
markers: Text in [verify] still needs checking against the source. Remove the tag once checked.
keyPoints: About **three-quarters** of people with psychosis have **overweight or obesity**, and up to **80%** in a first episode gain **≥7%** of body weight within a year [1].
**Choice of antipsychotic** is the most important risk factor. Clozapine and olanzapine carry the highest risk [2,1].
Give **diet and exercise** advice to everyone **from the day of prescribing** [3,1].

**Metformin:** start with olanzapine or clozapine; with quetiapine, risperidone or paliperidone if there is a cardiometabolic risk factor or age 10–25; with **any** antipsychotic if weight rises **>3% in the first year** [1].

clinicalFeatures.definition: Clinically significant weight gain is a rise of **≥7% from baseline body weight** [1]. Weight gain comes from more calorie intake, more appetite and a slower metabolism [3].

course.onset: Rapid in the **first weeks**; the first year is critical [1]
course.driver: **Choice of drug**, the strongest baseline factor [1]
course.reversible: Partly. Switching drug gives about **−1.5 kg** on average [1]

clinicalFeatures.consequences: Obesity doubles the risk of all-cause death, coronary heart disease, stroke and type 2 diabetes. Each 1 kg gained raises cardiovascular risk by about 3.1%. Weight gain is a leading cause of distress, and people with obesity are 2.5 times more likely to stop their medicine [1].

thresholds.value: Use a lower BMI threshold (**>23**) for South Asian, Chinese, Black African and African-Caribbean people [1]
HbA1c **42–47 mmol/mol** (6.0–6.4%) or fasting glucose **6.1–6.9 mmol/L** (110–125 mg/dL) [1]

riskFactors: **Choice of antipsychotic:** the most important non-genetic factor [1]
**Younger age:** children and adolescents gain up to twice as much as adults [1]
**First episode or antipsychotic-naive:** 3–4 times more weight gain [1]
**Early gain in weight or BMI:** the strongest predictor of long-term gain [1]

drugsImplicated.note: Antipsychotics [2]; other drugs [3]. Drugs not shown are not rated in these sources.
drugsImplicated.groupNote: First-generation antipsychotics other than chlorpromazine and haloperidol have little individual data; they are rated moderate as a group [2].

rows.maudsley: Baseline, frequently for 3 months, then yearly. Clozapine, olanzapine: 3-monthly in year 1.
rows.adaapa: Baseline, 4, 8 and 12 weeks, then quarterly. Waist: baseline, then yearly.

rows.maudsley: Baseline, then frequently during titration and dose changes.
Baseline, 4–6 months, then yearly. Clozapine, olanzapine, chlorpromazine: baseline, 1 month, then 4–6-monthly.
Baseline, 3 months, then yearly. Clozapine, olanzapine: 3-monthly in year 1.
rows.adaapa: Baseline, 12 weeks, then every 5 years if normal.

monitoring.ifAbnormal: If results are abnormal: lifestyle advice, consider changing the antipsychotic, and start a statin or refer as needed [2].

items: Give **diet and exercise** advice when prescribing, and continue it throughout [3,1].
Choose the **lowest-risk antipsychotic** that suits the patient, especially if BMI is already raised [3,1].
Use the **flowchart** below at the start of an antipsychotic or a switch [1].

**Switching** or lowering the dose: about **−1.5 kg** (95% CI −2.03 to −0.98) versus staying on the same drug. Clinical significance is uncertain, and switching is not possible for some, e.g. on clozapine [1].
**Adjunctive aripiprazole** (5–15 mg/day) added to clozapine gives modest weight loss [6].
Match treatment to **BMI class** and offer an **FDA-approved obesity medication** where indicated (below) [3,4].

flowchart.appliesTo: At the start of an antipsychotic, or a switch from one to another [1]

groups.condition: Any of: hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, prediabetes, BMI >25 (adjust for ethnicity), or age 10–25
>3% weight gain at any time in the first year (60 kg → 1.8 kg; 70 kg → 2.1 kg; 80 kg → 2.4 kg; 90 kg → 2.7 kg). Young people: >3% outside their growth trajectory.
BMI ≥30, or 27–30 with hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, prediabetes or obstructive sleep apnoea
groups.action: Start a GLP-1 agonist; metformin if not possible

flowchart.always: Diet and exercise for everyone, continued alongside metformin [1].

metformin.effect: Prevents about **3–4 kg** of gain when started with the antipsychotic; about **3 kg** loss in established gain [1].
metformin.howItWorks: Lowers appetite and liver glucose output and improves insulin response. It does not stimulate insulin secretion, so it does not cause hypoglycaemia [1].
tips: Take with or after food. Target **1–2 g/day** [1].
If GI side effects persist, use **slow-release once daily** [1].

sideEffects.effects: Transient nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, loss of appetite; vitamin B12 deficiency
Lactic acidosis; abnormal liver tests or hepatitis; skin reactions

avoid: Acute physical illness, or harmful alcohol use (**AUDIT ≥8**)
monitor: Symptoms of lactic acidosis: breathlessness, muscle cramps, abdominal pain, hypothermia, weakness
Renal function **yearly**; 6-monthly if over 75 or on NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs or diuretics
Vitamin B12 **yearly**; 6-monthly if vegan, after bariatric surgery, on a PPI or colchicine, older, or with malabsorption
stop: Suspected lactic acidosis, or risk of it: dehydration, acute alcohol intoxication, decompensated heart failure, respiratory failure, recent MI, shock, severe infection
Before or at iodinated contrast; restart at least **48 h** after
**Sick-day rule:** stop if systemically unwell, restart when well

obesityMedications.intro: FDA-approved obesity medications, with lifestyle change. Weight loss shown is beyond placebo [4].

rows.avoid: Severe GI disease; personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2. Reduces oral contraceptive efficacy.
Severe GI disease; personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2
Cardiovascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, glaucoma, hyperthyroidism
Uncontrolled hypertension, seizures, glaucoma, eating disorders, substance use disorder, chronic opioid use
Severe GI disease; personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2
Cardiovascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, glaucoma, hyperthyroidism, substance use disorder, agitated states

goals: **≥5%** sustained loss gives meaningful health benefit; **≥10%** for most obesity-related diseases; **≥15%** in some [4].
Follow up **monthly for 3 months**, then **3-monthly** in year 1, then **6-monthly** [4].
If **≥5%** is lost by 3 months, continue long term; stopping usually leads to regain [4].
Not in pregnancy, when trying to conceive, or when breastfeeding [4].
GLP-1 agonists in people with overweight or obesity, including antipsychotic-induced: about **−6 kg** (95% CI −10.8 to −1.36) [1].

otherOptions.notes: ≥10% weight gain in **17.8% vs 29.8%** on olanzapine alone at 24 weeks [7].

rows.treatment: Behavioural + medical weight management, or behavioural management + surgery

mechanism.intro: Clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine and mirtazapine block both **H1 and 5-HT2C** receptors [3]. Quetiapine's 5-HT2C blockade comes mainly from its active metabolite, norquetiapine. [verify]

diagrams.title: Appetite: H1 and 5-HT2C blockade
diagrams.start: Psychotropic with H1 and/or 5-HT2C blocking activity

branches.head: H1 blockade
items: More hypothalamic AMPK activity, which promotes feeding

branches.head: 5-HT2C blockade
items: Weaker appetite suppression through POMC neurons

join: More hunger and food intake, less energy spent on movement

diagrams.title: Leptin resistance
diagrams.context: Normally, leptin from fat cells activates POMC/CART neurons (α-MSH → MC4 receptors → less appetite) and inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons (less hunger).
diagrams.start: Psychotropic exposure and increasing body fat

branches.head: Reduced hypothalamic response to leptin: leptin resistance

join: More food intake → further fat gain, which worsens leptin resistance

diagrams.title: Peripheral metabolic effects
diagrams.start: Certain antipsychotics, particularly clozapine and olanzapine

branches.head: Weight-independent loss of insulin sensitivity
items: Muscle, liver and fat respond less to insulin; worsened by rising body fat

join: Poorer glucose control → hyperglycaemia and diabetes risk, sometimes before weight changes

diagrams.title: Gut microbiome
diagrams.note: Evidence is mostly from animal studies.

branches.head: Altered microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids
Possible change in energy extracted from food

join: Changes in metabolism and appetite regulation
More energy available for storage → weight gain

mechanism.metformin: Metformin may also reduce antipsychotic-induced metabolic dysfunction through the gut–brain axis; this evidence is emerging [3].

differentialDiagnosis: **Other weight-promoting medicines:** insulin, sulfonylureas, pioglitazone, beta-blockers, glucocorticoids, progestogen contraception, sedating antihistamines [4]
**Recovery of appetite** as depression or psychosis improves
**Lifestyle change:** less activity, diet, stopping smoking, alcohol

keyEvidence.finding: Mean gain at **10 weeks**: clozapine ~4.5 kg, olanzapine ~4.2 kg, risperidone ~2.1 kg, haloperidol ~1.1 kg, ziprasidone ~0.04 kg [9].
**30% on olanzapine** gained ≥7% of body weight, versus 7–16% on the other drugs [10].
Early psychosis, 52 weeks: ≥7% gain in **80%** on olanzapine, **58%** on risperidone, **50%** on quetiapine [11].
Started with risperidone or olanzapine: **−4.03 kg** (95% CI −5.78 to −2.28); low certainty [1].
Started with an antipsychotic: **−3.12 kg** (95% CI −4.22 to −2.01); very low certainty [1].
Cohort of 396: **−3.14 kg** at 6 months and **−5.38 kg** at 12 months; low certainty [1].

examPearls: Clinically significant weight gain is **≥7% of baseline weight** [1].
**H1 + 5-HT2C** blockers cause the most gain: clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine, mirtazapine [3].
**Bupropion** may be the only antidepressant that causes weight loss [3].
**Paroxetine** causes the most gain among SSRIs; TCAs and MAOIs cause more than SSRIs [3].
Among mood stabilisers, **divalproex, carbamazepine and lithium** cause the most gain; lamotrigine is weight-neutral; topiramate and zonisamide cause weight loss [3].
Insulin resistance can develop **independently of weight gain** [3].

selfTest.question: A 70 kg man starts aripiprazole for schizophrenia. He has no cardiometabolic risk factors. Four months later he weighs 72.6 kg. What is the best next step?

options.text: Recheck at 12 months; aripiprazole is low risk
Start metformin and continue diet and exercise advice

selfTest.explanation: He has gained 2.6 kg (3.7%), more than the >3% threshold (2.1 kg at 70 kg) in the first year, so the guideline recommends metformin even with a lower-risk antipsychotic. His BMI does not meet the GLP-1 criteria [1].
